What's the most ruthless thing a new boss has done to show he/she is in charge? My very first job was doing construction labor for my stepfather when I was 17. He was a foreman and a downright bastard of a foreman. The guys on the site would refer to him as Pharaoh. When I told him about that nickname he laughed heartily and seemed proud of himself. He worked everyone to the bone. He pretended he had the highest standards when he looked at the work his men did. He boasted that he helped construct mega projects in Brooklyn and Vermont and that the house that we were building must 'shine like his mansion' (even though in reality he lived in a wooden shack with no electricity as my mother had recently kicked him out. The men all respected him though. There wasn't a job that he cussed out a laborer or mason for that he couldn't do himself. For a thin, wiry 5′9 guy he was full of strength and energy. He loved to display this whenever he claimed we were taking too long and would grab someone's shovel and mix mortar or concrete effortlessly as though he was whipping up mashed potatoes. He once gave me the duty of tearing down a large 10ft mound of earth and then transporting the dirt to fill behind a retaining wall. All day I spent labouring and when the sun began to set, barely half of the mound was done. It was too solid for me to break. He dropped some F and C bombs at me, grabbed my pickaxe and with a few solid strikes the mound was no more. I was utterly stunned. However he was utterly provocative, insensitive and and sometimes seemed borderline insane. He would get into these mood swings and yell at us to get off our lazy c**ts and work even if a heavy shower of rain was falling. He wanted to pick a fight with a mason when none of the bricks were laid, not realising that the bricks weren't delivered to the site yet. He would stamp around ceaselessly yelling the F word whenever there was a setback, even if it was no fault of the workers. Sometimes we wondered if he was on drugs. He seemed to have an intense hatred of seeing his workers do nothing and in his tantrums he would flings brooms and buckets our way commanding us to ‘dont sit and gape, clean the f**king place or something.' But all of this were just gimmicks to stoke fear and intimidate everyone. He believed that in his field that was the only way to get the job done. However, the worst thing he ever did to instill fear and show power was when he forced the laborers (mostly young, naive men like myself) to climb planks of wood to get to the foundation floor. He thought it was better than spending money renting some scaffolding. One of the new laborers (a young man who seemed mentally slow) fell off the planks while carrying bricks and received an awful bleeding gash on his elbow, rendering him unable to work hard. Pharoah inspects the wound and gets angry. 'No, no no,' he said solemnly, “Just go. Get out of here.’ The young man pleaded that he could work but my stepfather fired him on the spot, without as much care as to offering a bandaid. Looking at the guy I could see that he came from poverty and probably had little to no education, let alone the fact that he was mentally slow. I thought the rest of the labourers would revolt against him for their friend but Pharoah knew how to please his peons. Beers. Every Friday he treated the boys to drinks on his bill after work at a bar in the closest town. The men would get stone drunk and cheer to their master. They never realised that some of the money he used to buy these drinks was the money he made off cutting costs and overworking them.

If you could choose only one font which one would it be and why? Without a doubt Gill Sans. Something about these World War II era fonts stirs up romantic and escapist feelings within my subconscious. From these ugly times came this beautiful, almost flawless font. I’m no anglophile but the British (specifically Eric Gill employed at the prestigious Monotone company) knew a thing or two about subtlety, graceful curvature and ‘breathing space’ when it came to eye-catching typefaces. Symmetry is the essence of being and Gill Sans makes every effort to be symmetrical yet bold and demanding. It is referred to as a ‘humanist’ font, in that it is easily legible in text and display to the extent that lines do not overlap or meld into each other. Intricate focus is put on the roundness of its letters, most notably, having a perfect circle for the ‘O’ Gill Sans, to me, conjures up images of RAF fighter planes heading eastwards in formation, Orwell interviewing coal miners at their last breath due to tuberculosis, children in rags catching colored butterflies amidst the rubble of buildings blown to pieces in Dresden and the decay of British Raj. Terrible times indeed but captured in various newspapers, flyers and magazines with this pleasant font which made many nations feel hope for better times to come.

What are the things no one tells you about living alone? That it gradually transforms you into someone who WANTS to be alone. If you are like me and have just a drop of introvert blood in you, living alone becomes like an introvert blood transfusion. Or, as I like to call it, an introversion. When you're accustomed hanging out with groups of diverse friends, hearing about the different lifestyles , perceptions and life choices of others, not only does empathy and understanding come naturally but also a desire to empathize and understand people around you grows. If you don't do this regularly, you feel awkward and incomplete. It becomes a subconscious necessity the same way people who have a gym routine tend to always have to be at the gym otherwise they'll be in an awful mood. When you live with someone your mind gravitates towards the study and understanding of the person/persons living with you. Whether it be your spouse, children, sibling, in-law, friend, roommate etc, you naturally become preoccupied studying such an individual and the gears of human nature are in motion in that you become naturally interested in people as a whole. When you live alone, your mind becomes preoccupied with itself and your own interests, likes and dislikes, theories and experiences. Your ability to empathize lessens greatly and you find yourself easily irritated and avoiding people who do not share the same mindset as yours (practically the rest of the world). You've become so used to expending energy inwards that it becomes a Herculean effort to try and get to know others. You'd rather not pretend to be glad about Megan's new boyfriend (who sounds like a piece of s**t) or grudgingly compliment Billy on his decision to take his kids to Disneyland rather than pay off his arrears for the car or be pressured into attending the church cake sale when you're secretly an atheist. Living alone makes you that person who just doesn't want to make that effort to get to know the people around you. Getting to know people seems about as difficult and exhausting as someone with physique of Gandhi trying to do the workout of a prime Arnold Schwarzenegger. Unless you are a natural recluse, living alone is not a good idea for the reasons stated above. But hey that's just my two cents.

Are there parents who regret having mixed-race children? My paternal grandfather Anthony Roy Hughes was a white Grenadian and his wife Mona (paternal grandmother) was a mixed raced Grenadian. Together they had six children and enjoyed an upper middle class existence after they both migrated to Trinidad, him working for Shell Oil and her working as a French school teacher. They bought a large house together in a picturesque neighborhood called Cascade. Things were definitely not as happy as it appears in the above photos. Grandfather was abusive with untreated manic depression/bipolar symtoms. It was said by my family that he never truly loved my grandmother. His original goal was to find a white wife (as was the norm during colonial times) and she was the closest thing he could get towards that goal. It was also said that he gave preferable treatment to his more Caucasoid children and was particularly unloving to the others who weren't (my father [center of the above photo] being a prime target due to his being the darkest of the lot). In just a few years within the marriage he lost his job at Shell Oil as being seen as unfit. Despite being given a severance payout he depended on his wife's teaching salary to provide for him and the children. Jobless and prone to depressive episodes he would make every attempt to find merriment outside of his home and when he did come home his frustrations over his incapacities and failures were taken out on his wife and children. My aunt would tell me that they would hear him singing drunken songs as he came up the hill towards the house and according to what song he sang, they would know whether he was ready to give everyone a whupping or if he would go shut himself in his bedroom for several hours. They prayed that it would be the latter. He depended on his wife's salary and her kind nature to hold the family together, pay the bills and take care of the house. Meanwhile he repaid her kindness by being more physically and emotionally abusive. Grandma was stricken with motor neuron disease in her early 40s and wasted away wheelchair bound for the last years of her life, passing away at the relatively young age of 48. All this tragedy and abuse contributed to their children suffering from various neuroses and mental illnesses. Only two managed to have some measure of success in their personal lives while the rest succumbed to directionless lives of struggle and financial and mental hardships, the youngest committing suicide at age 40 and two recently passing away alone and in squalor. But rather than delve into personal history (and there's a lot), let me answer the original question. Are there parents who regret having mixed-raced children? It is possible that my grandfather regretted his mixed raced children and harbored deep prejudices. It is also possible that he loved his mixed race children but his untreated mental illness brought out the worst in him. The answer in regards to my grandfather is probably. He showed no remorse when his wife died, relieved himself of any further fatherly duties and made no attempt to establish communication with his children. He sold the house and remarried (his long sought after white bride) a few years after his first wife's death. He died a lonely divorcée in 1994. Would he have made a greater effort to be a better father if he had found his white bride and had a flock of children, all the same complexion as him? No one knows.

What is an example of an album that, in your opinion, was ruined by the producer and/or the production? It always blows my mind why no one mentions how awfully inconsistent the sound is in Jimi Hendrix's legendary Are You Experienced album. Not saying that it's a bad album, it's one of the greatest albums on Earth. However I can't help but shudder when I hear sound inconsistencies and downright amateurish recording. It's so sad that someone like Hendrix who was possibly the greatest guitarist of the 20th century had his masterpiece recorded in mono. His complex arrangements condescended to just a flat block of sound. Worse yet, because of financial burden, Chas Chandler, the producer and member of The Animals, had the album recorded in 16 different sessions at 3 different locations. When you go from track to track you can hear the chaos behind the production. Songs like Manic Depression, Stone Free and May This Be Love sound hollow as though recorded in someone's basement whilst Fire, Purple Haze and Hey Joe are treated with tender loving care. Love or Confusion sounds as though Chandler was tripping acid while recording and simply toying with the mix as within a few seconds the volume suddenly increases in itself erratically and from then on it's a brawl between guitar, bass and drums. In many instances the Hendrix's voice and guitar overwhelms Mitch Mitchell's drums and Noel Reddings bass. As much as I love Hendrix and his guitar prowess, he wasn't the greatest of vocalists and some tracks could of benefitted with greater accentuation of his talented bandmates. All in all, the chaotic production behind Are You Experienced makes it feel more like a collection of B sides (exceptional B sides) rather than a work of art. Each track takes me to a different place, but not in a good way. I'm sure this wasn't the ‘Experience’ Hendrix wanted the world to have, but say what, it's still an excellent album.

What screams "I make terrible financial decisions!"? I worked with a lady in her early 40s at a pizza restaurant. She was just a ordinary grunt like the rest of us. She aspired to be a supervisor but what held her back was that she had 6 kids, three, in their late teens/early adulthood for one father, another two of toddler age for another father and a baby for her recent boyfriend. This domestic situation made it hard for her punctuality and regularity at work as there was always a babysitting issue or child maintenance issue that needed resolving with her two exes. Her current boyfriend was no supportive stalwart himself as practically once every week she would stop her duties to go outside the restaurant to have long and intense arguments with him on the phone in regards to his inability to come pick her up that evening or various other disagreements that they had. In person the boyfriend had a nasty, arrogant attitude and seemed to care only for casual sex, his car and for her to keep his baby away from her older kids whom they all shared a mutual dislike with one another. She lived with her two toddlers and her baby at her father's house which was shared with several other siblings of similar circumstance. With that there was a lot of family fighting in regards to space and ownership. To put it bluntly she lived in a world of shit. Given the circumstances it seemed unlikely that she would be unable break free from the poverty and drudgery any time soon. I would feel the greatest sympathy for her and try my best to help her at work in any regards. That is until that fateful day when I saw her rubbing her stomach and smiling to herself. ‘Looks like you're ready for another one (baby)’ I said jokingly. She smiled and said that she and her current boyfriend (the arrogant dickhead) was trying for another baby. They had a girl and now he wanted a boy. ‘Are you serious?’ I said. I was flabbergasted that she was saying this so casually. It was as if she suddenly reverted back to a naive 16 yr old who found her first love and was no longer a middle aged woman with 6 children and a truckload of problems. One of my biggest flaws is that sometimes I can't keep my opinions to myself. ‘But you have 6 kids already!’ For a second she came out of her dream and reverted back to reality. She glared at me angrily for a split second .Then she returned to her child like persona and replied, ‘Children are a blessing.’ ‘Children are a blessing when you can afford to raise them right and give them the love and attention they need.’ Those words just came out of me in very emphatic tone. As a father of one (I worked part time at the restaurant) I was struggling to survive, working two jobs to ensure that my daughter had a future and to ensure all of my free time was dedicated to her. This lady worked one job and was dependent on family, friends and the Government to assist with any shortcomings she encountered, which seemed to be every day. I could not relate at all to what she was saying. She glared at me again and the conversation ended. An hour later I'm called into the manager's office. Apparently she got so angry she complained to the manager that I was being emotionally abusive, chauvinistic (the restaurant was 90% female staff) and stuck my nose in other people's business. She even told the manager that my words were so hurtful she felt overcome with hurt that she was considering taking a sick day and leaving. I sat and nodded in silence. I was the given a warning and sent out of the office. I learned a sad but valuable lesson that day: Some people are simply destined for a life of hardship and misery through their own stubborn mentality and poor choices. So to answer the question What screams "I make terrible financial decisions!"?: People who get offended by the truth.

Can you name an actor who was never a good actor but became one? Sterling Hayden never wanted to be an actor. He was coaxed into the profession as a young, handsome sailor whose photogenic good looks appealed to a post WWII audience who were just begging for actors who were the image of tall and rugged manliness. The 6′5 blonde, athletic young shipmate got into the industry after a 1938 photo gained popularity in a fisherman's magazine. Dubbed by Paramount as 'The Beautiful Blond Viking God’ he got into the industry as a means to purchase his own ship but grew to resent Hollywood. His early roles were a slew of rather forgettable Westerns and film noirs. After his role in the classic Western Johnny Guitar starring Joan Crawford he became a bonafide star. However around this time his personal life got more attention as he was reported to have communist sympathies during the McCarthy/Red Scare era and during a vicious custody battle for his children he took his four children on a self manned trip aboard his ship Wanderer from San Francisco Bay to Tahiti despite the legal implications that awaited him at home. His impulsive nature, hatred of Hollywood,anti- capitalism sentiments and sometimes reckless behaviour gave him the image of an eccentric, of which is well documented in his autobiography Wanderer (1963). However upon working with Stanley Kubrick in The Killing he found his niche playing manic and impulsive characters, not far removed from his actual personality. His best role arguably being that of the insane American General Jack D. Ripper in Kubrick's classic black political comedy Dr. Strangelove. His final great role was that of corrupt Irish police Captain Mark McCluskey in The Godfather (1972). Despite the critical and commercial resurgence his roles and his writings were used solely to fund his travels of which (along with legal expenses and taxes) he continuously saw his money decrease. He died of prostate cancer at the of 70 in 1986, leaving behind six children.

What television shows started strong only to become unwatchable later? Skins (2007 - 2013) The show was highly popular with millennials as it strove to give a realistic depiction of teenaged adults of that generation. The show, with its graphic portrayal of promiscuous sex and drug use among the majority of its main cast made it controversial at the time. Themes such as anorexia, poverty, depression, trauma, dysfunctional parenting etc were also touched on without succumbing to preaching or caricature. In essence the show was a comedy that subtly touched on some of the drama that went on in the personal lives of each of its characters. Generation 1 Without a doubt the first generation of Skins (Series 1 -2) is the true representation of the show. The first two seasons chronicles the lives of the above 9 teenagers. I enjoyed how no one was treated as the star of the show. Everyone had their positive traits as well as deep seated flaws but no one is given more screen time over the other or made into a token. The show focused on the youths as a group rather than as an hierarchy. The lifestyle may have been a tad exaggerated in its insistence that every character supposedly engaged in promiscuous sex and/or drug use. Besides that the show was an honest representation of teenaged millennials, written by an actual millennial, Jamie Brittain, who was 22 at the premier of the first season. The show launched the careers of actors Nicholas Hoult and Dev Patel who portrayed Tony and Anwar respectively. Generation 2 The second generation of Skins (Series 3–4) saw some changes. The comedic tone was increased as well as the amount of sex. The third season started off with an air of superficiality compared to the first generation but had a few well written moments and thoughtful episodes, particularly that of the trials and tribulations of teenaged Congolese immigrant Thomas. However the cast seemed all over the place and without developed characterization except that of cheap stereotypes (bully, geek, skater boy, drama queen, femme fatale etc.) Unlike Generation 1, this generation seemed to have an hierarchy among the cast as everything seemed to revolve around the characters Effy and Cook, who were, unsurprisingly, the most promiscuous and morally unscrupulous of the lot. Nearing the end of series 3 the show's writing started to wear thin. Shocks, drama and comedy were shoehorned in at every chance available. The show and its characters started losing their sense of direction and some of the themes that made them compelling characters in the beginning were abandoned in favour of sex and silliness. Some episodes were so ludicrous it became an effort to keep my eyes on the screen. The show seemed like a poor man’s imitation of itself. (So he's stealing a boat now…?) By series 4 it became painful to watch and I gave up. I have no intention to watch the third generation nor the American MTV remake. However the first generation of Skins remains a classic in my mind and a damned brilliant character study. It's hard for any writer to keep such a momentum going so you got to give the creators of the show credit for trying, even if they tried too hard in the end.

What's the worst experience you've had with telling someone you had feelings for them? While at University I observed that any course that had the word 'Management’ within its name was bound to be laden with beautiful women. When I did Management Accounting I was introduced by Lorna, a good female friend of mine, to this tall, shapely and somewhat quirky young lady with thick black curls, full lips and a shapely body. The only flaw that I observed was she had a slight paunch. Her name was Gabrielle or Gabby as she preferred to be called. She had an outspoken yet aloof disposition whereby she could say the most unfiltered thing and it would never come across offensive, well to me at least. I recall while walking with her and Lorna, Gabby randomly blurted out that my fantasy would be for her and Lorna to carry me to some secret location for a lapdance and ménage à trois. Lorna went red, either in anger, embarassment or a combination of the two. I soon discovered that Gabby's sister attended the school where I worked. I was never able to procure Gabby's phone number as I never got another chance encounter (she was very delinquent in class attendance) and Lorna didn't have it either. I then came up with what I considered a fool proof idea. I would write an old fashioned love letter, explaining my feelings for her and sealed with a kiss I would carry it to her sister to have it delivered to Gabby. All my feelings just flowed out of me as I wrote that long letter. I put a sticker of a rose and then neatly folded it into a red envelope. When I came upon the sister (12 years old at the time) I explained to her my feelings for Gabby and my intention for her to deliver this letter of love to her. I was expecting the sister to gush and swoon (as girls her age are prone to do regarding such romance) but instead she gave me an odd look of confusion and disbelief. 'Are you sure?’ Was all she could reply. 'Yeah,' I said flatly, 'Your sister made such an impression on me. I can't stop thinking of her.’ 'Why don't you just tell her yourself?’ the sister replied in that off-putting, emotionless tone quite strange for a girl her age. 'I don't have her phone number,' I replied and after a brief silence where I'm sure the sister sized me up and decided not to give me Gabby's number, she acquiesced to delivering the letter. The following day, I went up to the sister anxious to hear of what was Gabby's response or better yet collect a letter of my own. 'Did you give her the letter? I asked excitedly. The sister avoided my glances. 'Yeah.' I waited for her response. 'And what happened?’ I said, detecting a faint feeling that this wasn't going to work out well. 'She just looked at it and asked who it was from.’ Another silence. 'And what happened after?’ I said with an underlying sense of dread. 'She asked me what it was you wanted. I told her that you liked her…..she looked at the letter and then put it on her dresser.’ I felt my stomach tighten. 'Didnt she read the letter?’ 'No,' the sister flatly replied, 'She still hasn't opened it.’ There was an awkward silence and the sister then uttered, 'Sir I have to go.’ I felt like the world's biggest clown. I half imagined the sister running to tell a her classmates what a loser Mr. Williamson was and then describing the story. Fast forward four months later and I'm shopping around for car insurance. I head into this big building and none other than Gabby is sitting at the reception office, heavily pregnant. She engages me in delightful quirky conversation as normal almost as though the whole love letter incident was a figment of my imagination. I bid her adieu and immediately called Lorna to tell her what happened to her friend. 'My friend!’ Lorna said shocked, 'She wasn't my friend. She's just a girl from my class. I thought she was your friend! Didn't you realize she was pregnant?’ I replied no and then explained my prior feelings for Gabby and the whole love letter fiasco. 'You sent Gabby a love letter!’ Lorna cried in great shock, 'But she's pregnant….and she's engaged. Didn't you see the ring on her finger?’ Suddenly I just felt like a massive brick landed on my head. Soon the pieces started to fit together.

Which character did you view totally differently as a child vs. as an adult? Roy Neary - Close Encounters of the Third Kind If there is one character who deserves the award for biggest douchebag protagonist Richard Dreyfuss’ performance of Roy Neary wins that award by a wide margin. He's a blue collar, salt of the Earth electrician, an honest man with a loving wife and two kids. While driving home at night he has an encounter with UFOs and his life suddenly changes dramatically. Without giving away too much of the story I'll concentrate on his character. As a child I saw Roy Neary as a hero, a distressed and eccentric one but a hero nonetheless. He worked relentlessly to uncover a secret Government rendezvous between humans and aliens about to happen in his area. He overcame all obstacles set forward by the Government, the army, secret service and his own family leaving him to prove himself right; that aliens and UFOs did indeed exist and the Government was indeed staging a landmark meeting between man and intelligent extraterrestrial life forms. Roy takes it even a step further. In the final moments of the movie he offers himself to the aliens and boards their ship amidst dozens of alien children. We are then treated to a rousing score accompanied by the beautiful flashing lights of the mothership as it majestically floats off into the sky and the credits roll. It is a fantastic scene full of wonder and innocence that only the likes of Spielberg could deliver. The End That is how I saw the film as a child. As an adult it was a completely different experience. Roy Neary was this a-hole who could give two farts about his wife and kids and all his responsibilities in life. His family didn’t leave him because they were impatient with his alien obsession, in fact they were remarkably patient with his bullshit. He stopped working and stopped caring about anything that didn’t involve anything regarding secret Government cover ups and aliens. However when he begins thrashing the house to build a model Devil’s Tower mountain and becoming a threat to himself, his family and neighbours are they forced to evacuate the premises in a state of trauma. Some people theorize that Roy was under some sort of mind control by the aliens and his actions were not willfully done, that everything was planned and coordinated by the alien masterminds. I argue that Roy was just a big A-hole. Why would the aliens have Roy come close to sabotaging the secret meeting with his annoying shenanigans? Roy acts with little intelligence and self control throughout most of the movie. He's like a selfish, impetulant and irresponsible child that must be the first in line to get the latest Playstation in stores. He has an ‘Us and them’ mentality whereby if you weren't an actual UFO witness or some half-cracked alien conspiracy theorist he didn't care about what you said and law and order didn't exist. I think Roy is a big stain on a great movie. When you think about it, none of his actions benefited anyone. Jillian would've gotten back her son regardless if she went Devil's Tower or not and his discovery would amount to nothing because no one would believe him afterwards. He ruined his family all so he could see some cool alien stuff and weasel his way into the heart of a grieving single mom. His character is supposed to be redeemed by offering himself to the aliens. To me he is just this UFO geek that wanted to escape paying child support. Lacombe: Monsieur Neary. You can't go aboard zat space sheep. What about your madame and infants? Neary:……my work here is done.

What’s your relationship with alcohol? As a self-described connoisseur of fine liquor I have to honestly say that my relationship with alcohol has reached something of a close. In my mid to late 20s, when I started to drink habitually, one stiff drink used to give me a solid buzz/near drunkenness that lasted a couple hours. A 750ml bottle of rum, vodka, whisky or scotch with a chaser of choice could last me a month and change. However this frugality was because I had little alcohol tolerance and was prone to hangovers. Excessive drinking was not greatly desired unless I had friends over or something to celebrate. In my early to mid 30s, what I consider my peak age of drinking, two stiff drinks gave me a solid buzz and anything over that got me into the tipsy/drunken spectrum. This lasted about two hours at most and I had great tolerance. Hangovers ceased to exist for me, partially due to experience but mostly due to self discipline. However my urge to drink started growing and I started to feel come downs more strongly and frequently. Now I’m in my late 30s. It takes me three stiff drinks to get a solid buzz that lasts 30 minutes to an hour. After this my come down lasts practically the rest of the evening and lingers into the next day. The urges are so strong that sometimes the first place I'm drawn to in a grocery is the liquor section. A 750ml bottle wouldn't last me more than a week at the height of my urges. The funny thing about alcohol is that when I reach that peak whereby my buzz is at its strongest but I've not yet condescended into drunkenness, I feel as though I’ve manifested into my supreme self. It tricks me into thinking my mind operates deeper and much more efficiently under its influence. The day I found on my phone a ‘supreme self’ video recording I did of me slurring and rambling about deep, self discoveries through alcohol, it did me a favour and proved otherwise. I'm not a shitty person when I'm drunk. Nobody has a problem with me intoxicated. I've never become uncouth, aggressive or self destructive when I drink. I'm a shitty person during the come down. I become sullen, withdrawn and easily irritated. I lose sight of my goals and ambition and I tend to focus on all my disappointments in life which opens the floodgate to anxiety and depression. I've come to the stage where alcohol takes away a lot more than it gives. Yeah, the occasional beer or cocktail makes me feel relaxed, temporarily kicks out my fears and anxieties and can even give me a boost of confidence but now I’ve found myself at an odd stage in my life where my body is both desirous of alcohol and yet repelled by it. As such I've been weaning off of harder liquor and instead been having an occasional drink of my own homemade fruit wines when the urges come. My wines are admittedly less than stellar and with an alcohol percentage so low it makes Coors Light look like absinthe. However even though weaning from alcohol has stopped me from feeling like Alexander the Great for an hour or so, it sure beats feeling like Eeyore the Donkey for hours on end afterwards.

Do biracial people ever pick their white side and identify as white? Sigh The above photo shows five mixed raced men of varying ethnic makeup, myself included. Which one do you think would be the most likely to identify as ‘white?’ If you chose the guy on the far left, congratulations, you have a talent to point out the obvious. That's my cousin. We all are. He is mixed race but looks ‘white.’ Growing up he never picked his white side, society picked it for him. Trinidad has a very small ‘Caucasian’ minority and as such he has been identified as one by the public and has grown to accept and embrace that identification. In the real world nobody wants to hear what you identify yourself as. You don't pick whether you are white or black, society does. If you try to challenge society’s label and argue that you are white when you look black or that you are black when you look white, you end up losing a lot of time, wasting a lot of energy and not to mention, irritating a lot of people with a topic that is intrinsically pointless. So whether you identify as white, black, male, female, young, old, binary, non-binary, here's some news for you: No one cares. No one is really listening. Nothing has changed.

What actor’s acting style has aged the worst? 'Why can't there be more talented actors like…like Steve Guttenberg?’ That's a conversation you've probably never heard. If anyone ever tells me that Officer Mahoney was their favorite character in Police Academy I'll regard him/her with Cold War level suspicion. He's not a bad actor. It's just that he plays the same cocky, smug bastard who rides off the charisma of all his talented co-stars and only offers an eerie, wry smile in return. When that fails he would then take off his shirt. He was never funny yet he had top billing in some of the biggest comedies of his time. He was never sexy yet he was always cast as some sort of ladies man. A typical Steve Guttenberg scene is as such: 'Character x does or says something hilarious……..Guttenberg takes centre stage and smiles.’ Or Something serious happens…..Guttenberg gives that ‘I hope no one noticed that I just farted’ look. A true product of his time. Sadly (for him) he all but vanished in the 21st century. But say what, we got a great joke about the Guttenberg phenomenon from The Simpsons. Edit 10.01.22. God rest his soul. This actor’s untimely death was both tragic and epic at the same time. Many say that he left the planet the way he wanted to. Click here to see who I’m talking about.

Who are the most uncomfortable movie characters depicting the UK that you’ve ever seen? Gotta go with three films and I'm listing the characters based on the level of discomfort (low to high). *** Spoilers ahead *** Movie: Saturday Night and Sunday Morning (1960) Character(s): Arthur Location: Nottingham The late, great Albert Finney gives a magnificent performance as Arthur, a rebellious, young, working class man who has somewhat of a fetish for stirring up trouble and going beyond the limit. The title refers to the fact that Arthur begins his trouble immediately after his work ends on Saturday. He dedicates his Saturday nights to going out pubs and drinking himself beyond consciousness, stirring up trouble in the streets, fighting etc. His Sundays are spent engaging in a sexual affair with the equally defiant wife of his mild-mannered co-worker. He eventually gets her pregnant while hiding his deeds from his own morally virtuous girlfriend. In the final scene Arthur confesses his actions to his girlfriend who forgives him and gets him to agree to marry her and settle down. Arthur agrees but angrily throws a stone at a nearby building. His girlfriend asks 'What did you do that for?’ He replies, 'Just felt like it I suppose.’ I don't live in the UK but I know and have befriended many Arthurs throughout my life here in Trinidad. Arthurs can never find inner peace and unknowingly to themselves, foster a subconscious hatred towards structure, routine and normalcy. They believe that a stone must be thrown into the rolling cogs every so often otherwise life would just be uneventful and monotonous. At their best Arthurs can be just angry, resentful troublemakers but at their worst they can be psychopathic narcissists who cause harm and destruction to all those who engage with them. Arthur in this film was a downright bastard in this kitchen-sink classic and anyone not interested in him as a character study would simply find him mildly repugnant. Movie: Kill List (2011) Character(s): Jay Location: Sheffield Kill List is something of a psychological/supernatural horror inspired by the fiction of HP Lovecraft. However there's nothing fictional about the character Jay. He's a menacing, angry and uncouth ex-soldier turned contract killer, quite possibly suffering from PTSD from a botched mission. He has a son and a wife who urges him to take a normal job as they are in financial distress but Jay prefers to wait for that one big contract job that would provide for him for years to come. His 'luck’ arrives as a friend of his wife hires him to eliminate various unnamed people in a mysterious Kill List. Jay and his friend are given locations of the targets The Priest, The Librarian and The MP. Each kill becomes more mysterious than the last with both of the first two victims softly thanking Jay before being killed. The 2nd kill unearths video evidence of an underground society involved in the most, depraved and disturbing acts imaginable causing Jay to become even more unsettled. Jay's final kill leads him to a mansion where a some sort of pagan cult is taking place with several figures hidden in white robes are having a ceremony. Believing these to be the people involved in the depraved videos he starts shooting them, killing some and manages to kill the leader. However he is captured and forced to a knife-fight with a robed hunchback figure. Viciously stabbing the hunchback all over its body, it is revealed afterwards to be his wife with their son strapped to her back. His final kill was his own family. I believe Kill List to be a portrayal of a man with psychosis and schizophrenia brought on by severe PTSD. Neil Maskell gives a phenomenal performance as Jay. His consistently scowling face and venemous tone make him such an unsettling character that I fear ever running into such a person on a lonely side street at night. I may be wrong but I interpret a lot of the happenings to be solely in Jay's imagination. Jay saw his own killings as something as a grand mission against evil so as to erase guilt from a botched mission in Kyiv where he, quite possibly, had to do heinous acts to survive. Kill List, to me, is a heightened portrayal of a mentally unstable man. Movie: Eden Lake (2008) Character(s): The parents Location: London Condemned by critics for stereotyping and exaggerating the 'Broken Britain’ underclass this film is relentless in its portrayal of savagery. Jenny and Steve are a couple vacationing and decide a visit a lake near a working class community. Steve is highly critical of the behaviour of the children of the area and the parents' role in their poor upbringing. Even though the lake is condemned to become a quarry Steve and Jenny sneak in for a final visit but become targets of a gang of local delinquent 'Chavs’ driven by a maniacal leader Brett. After constantly being harassed by the youths, a fight ensues in which Brett's dog is killed. Enraged he eventually raises the stakes by capturing Steve and having members of the group stab him to death while being filmed. Jenny is then captured and with botched attempts to kill her as well, Brett murders two of his own gang members while the rest look on silently. In the ensuing chase two other members of the gang are killed. Bleeding to near death and dirty, Jenny manages to run to a nearby house where a house party involving several middle aged locals are taking place. There is copious drug, alcohol and sex among the members and even though it is certain that these people are not her cup of tea she seeks help from one of the more sympathetic women. However she soon realises that many of them are parents of the gang and when one of the women get a police call informing of her murdered son, the parents suspect her and suddenly transform into 'we look after our own’ monsters. As far fetched as Brett and the gang is portrayed, I believe a good job was done portraying the parents. There are so many communities of families out there who have vague morals in regards to greater society but a strict code of secrecy and loyalty for themselves. Despite many of the horrific scenes in the movie, nothing was more uncomfortable and disturbing than this final scene. There is no major onscreen violence during the last five minutes but just looking at Jenny hiding in the bathroom as she hears the voices of the parents of these monsters (learning of their dead kids) screaming in trauma and yelling in rage as she acknowledges the fact that they will soon kill her makes it the most uncomfortable scene I've ever witnessed in a film set in the UK.

Who’s your favorite redhead? Julianne Moore is like a Home Run for read heads around the world. Those elven features with her small but chiselled face, green eyes, thick flowing hair. They should put her face in the middle of the flag of Ireland.

What are the cleverest scams you have come across? Take a breath, grab a coffee if you may, and allow me to explain to you why we are called 'Tricky-dadians’ by the rest of the Caribbean. Band Ladies Around 2016 — 2018 a phenomenon occurred where sightings of these cultish ladies in heavy clothing similar to that of traditional Amish females were found throughout Trinidad. They were typically spotted at commercial areas such as malls and PriceSmarts (Costco) mostly at the parking lot. They were renowned for asking for your assistance with the rebuilding of their church. They claimed to do this with the purchase of their cheap rubber hand bands of which they would charge anything upwards of $20TT. If you refused to buy their generic, overpriced bands they would then initiate Phase 2 of their scheme which would be to overwhelm the victim with guilt with a pathos laden statement of 'Or maybe you could contribute just a small donation. Anything?’ They employed great acting skills and for many, seeing these harmless women in humble, old fashioned garb being constantly refused and rejected for their worthy cause tugged a few heartstrings. However, as with most scams, they got too greedy too fast. Their monthly appearances soon turned to weekly and then daily. Rather than target one location for the day and wrap up afterwards, it soon became clear that they began employing routes. A typical Band Lady route would be PriceSmart Chaguanas till 2pm, Trincity Mall until 6pm and PriceSmart Mausica until 9pm. They were noticed and mentioned by some of the populace but being that they were always pleasant and took 'no’ graciously, no one bothered to think twice about their scheme. However, the last straw was a rather desperate appearance at a CPL T20 cricket match (above photograph). Trinidad is very tolerant of beggars and we throw a blind eye towards scammers for the most part but for the Band Ladies, plying their scheme in the middle of a regional cricket match where national pride was at a peak, created an online outcry. Everyone suddenly posted a story, photo or recording of a dubious encounter with one of these Band Ladies and from that moment on they were no longer seen in public. Warning *Foul language*

What is the weirdest thing you've ever witnessed a parent do? Neil was a troubled student in a school I worked in. Ms. Harris was his mom. In Trinidad we joke about the stereotypical ‘oppressed’ single mom who never sees wrong in her kids. The ones trying their best to raise their kids in a Government project, running out of the house delirious and screaming with curlers in their hair, desperately prostrating to the neighborhood to stop the awful policemen from arresting their innocent son who happened 'in the wrong place at the wrong time' during a robbery/breaking and entering. Ms.Harris was the textbook definition of such a mom; loyal to her children to the point of fanaticism and delusion. However, what set her apart from moms like her in the neighborhood was her gift for theatre. Ms. Harris could dish out so much pathos and could reach to the deep place inside her soul, channelling genuine emotions like the flick of a light switch. Those who didn't know any better would get easily influenced by her performances. She used this talent especially to bail Neil out of trouble. Once, Neil and a group of friends were to be expelled for selling marijuana on school premises. Before this was officiated, Ms. Harris came and gave an impromptu performance in the school staff room. ‘ ……go right ahead and tear the heart away from this poor, black woman. I have nothing. Neil has nothing. Only the love of struggling mother at wits end; a poor, black woman with no avenue in this world. Take my son and blind him so he cannot see the pain in his mother's face as we accept the fate of this cruel world; the fate of all poor, black women. As silly as her rhetoric was, she ended up getting her way and Neil and his friends had the matter covered up by the Principal and the police who witnessed this poor, black woman prostrating desperately towards them. One of the Literature teachers was so impressed that she approached Ms. Harris and told her that she belonged to a group that were looking for talent for the upcoming National 'Best Village’ competition sponsored by the Ministry of Culture. It was basically like a talent show with a focus on cultural dance, poetry, drama and spoken word. There were great prizes to be won and even if she didn't win, it would allow for great opportunities for her in local theatre. Ms. Harris agreed and immediately went and submitted an application for the audition. The event was scheduled the following month. Ms. Harris was dead set on giving the performance of a lifetime. She wanted the Minister of Culture to give her a standing ovation. She forgot all about Neil's problems at school to focus on her upcoming performance. She wrote an epic play that revolved around an oppressed woman who makes the journey to the motherland. There was to be a spoken word segment, a short play and end in a song and dance finale, complete with drums, dancers in exquisite costumes and professional lighting. However Ms. Harris bit off far too much than she could chew. Her obessesion with perfecting her vision of the performance led to many disputes with the dancers, sound effects, music and lighting personnel and nearing the date of the competition most of the crew quit and she was hard-pressed to find people to replace them. The day of the audition arrived and almost the entire neighborhood flocked to the Community Center to see Ms. Harris’ performance of a lifetime. Unbeknownst to Ms. Harris, the Minister of Culture was not going to be there, rather just a sole talent scout. There was no need for the amount of spectacle that Ms. Harris had in mind. When her moment came, she was nowhere to be found. Several people tried to contact her on her cell phone but she was not answering. Thirty minutes passed and the talent scout became furious as he had other locations to visit. Ms. Harris then materialized looking out of breath. En route to leaving she stopped the scout in his tracks to tell him that she was ready to perform but if only he could give herself and her dancers ten minutes to get their costumes ready and another ten minutes for the sound and lighting guys to arrive. The talent scout told her to perform now or she would be eliminated from the competition. Ms. Harris then began to prostrate in front of him saying: ‘How can you be so cold? How can you look at a poor, black woman and tell her that you are going to eliminate her? What has the world come to when a poor, black woman has a door shut in her face by a rich, black man? How can you? How can you?’ Needless to say the talent scout was not impressed by Ms. Harris' impromptu performance and had her eliminated. She learned the first lesson in Theatre 101 that day; don't overdo it

What is one thing that all men hate? Yesterday I was at home. I couldn't attend work because my area had been flooded for the third time in a month. It was both nerve-wracking and boring being stuck in a house surrounded by water and fearful that the rain falls and the water gets higher and enters inside. I get a missed call. It's from a lady at work who is notorious for always wanting something. Practically every encounter I've had with her usually ends up with her saying 'I wanted to ask you about…… ’ Or 'Would it be alright if I…..’ Or 'Next Monday I wanted to……' In other words she wanted a favour from me. This is all fine and dandy but truly I only like to perform favours to people I consider friends. By no stretch of the imagination do I consider her a friend and the sheer volume of favours she's asked me over the years is exponentially greater than the favours every friend of mine has ever asked me combined. I decided to not take the call. Moments later I see that she sends a voice message. I call my girlfriend and discuss whether I should ignore it and she tells me. 'What if the lady just wants to know if you're alright?’ I then feel guilty. Maybe I am being a bit cynical. I decide to listen to the voice message. I play it; 'Hi. Didn't see you in work today. Hope everything is ok….’ In my mind I said my girlfriend was right and I shouldn't be so presumptuous. However, I then hear a sentence that makes me recoil. 'Since you're not here I was wondering if I could use your office to….’ I stopped listening. I didn't reply. I think every single man would agree that we hate when people only seek after us to get favours done.

What was the "I'm done" moment in your last relationship? I have a 7 year old daughter with my ex. Our relationship was problematic to say the least and for the sake of being allowed to see my daughter I allowed for this 'hanging on a thread’ type relationship to persist for the majority of my daughter's life. My ex (M) and I never communicated well when it came to money. To make a long story short she decided to move out and furnish an apartment of her own whilst I concentrated on getting a house built. My ex had never had her own place and was extremely proud of the fact that she had her own place. To show how proud she was she furnished her apartment with the best television, stereo and appliances that money could buy. For my daughter's birthday I would usually come over with cake, ice cream and the like and we would have a small affair. However two days before my daughter's 6th birthday M calls me and this is the conversation that made me realize that I was done. M: 'I'm having a birthday party for Adrianna.’ Me: 'OK? (pondering why she didn't tell me in advance). Who's coming?’ M: 'My friends from work, my sisters and their children and my mother…..I invited your father too. I am buying the cake and pizza. What are you buying?’ Me: '……..so you told my father about this before you told me?’ M: (Getting noticeably irritated) 'Are you coming or not?’ Me: 'I would've appreciated it if you told me this in advance.’ M: 'So you're saying you don't want to have anything to do with your daughter's birthday?’ Me: 'I never said that.’ M: 'Go f**k yourself.’ She then hangs up the phone. I take some time to compose myself. I was not going to be forced to pay unnecessary money for M's vanity party so she could show off her apartment to her friends and family. In the end I didn't get to see Adrianna on her birthday. I came afterwards to drop my gift and wish her a belated birthday. Instead of expressing remorse over her attitude, M makes inflammatory and untrue comments about how cheap my gift was. I used to tell myself to keep faith and with enough effort M would finally warm over and show more love and respect. However that experience demonstrated that such an ideal would only lead to further pain, disrespect, abuse and her using our daughter as a weapon to get what she wants. The thread finally broke.

What was a red flag that made you stop talking to a person immediately? My brother had a relative staying over at his apartment and she brought along a friend. They both had just turned 18 and had recently run off from home (Red Flag #1) and were crashing at my brother's place basically sleeping all day and partying all night to their teenaged wont. I struck up a conversation with the friend (let's just call her Alice for simplicity's sake) and found her quite intelligent and charming despite her lifestyle. Went with Alice to hang out one night and we ended up in a club. We began dancing but I was quite surprised how physically close she positioned herself while we danced as we had only just met a week ago (Red Flag #2). I then asked her about how it was staying with my brother and she began a slew of insults as towards my brother's manners and housekeeping standards (Red Flag #3) despite the fact that she didn't help with his bills or rent. We exchanged numbers and I dropped her off home. She laid on her charm quite thick the entire journey and spoke of how great of a guy I was and that she couldn't wait for us to chat again. We exchanged numbers and the following morning I called her to see how she was doing. In a groggy voice she said ‘Who is this?’ I told her my name and to my surprise she said in a irritated tone, ‘Who? How did you get my number?’ (Red Flag #4) I reminded her that she gave me her number willingly the night before. She tried to laugh it off as being hung over. I reminded her that she only had one drink last night (Red Flag #5). There was an awkward silence and she tried to coo about how great of a guy I was but I cut her short and said that I was getting another call. Three years later Alice got pregnant for her boyfriend's married boss.

What is the strangest thing a truck driver has seen while driving? I'm cheating a bit. It was a pickup truck but I was hauling a long distance furniture delivery so technically it still counts. My loader Chris and I were on the highway when suddenly a spooked chicken ran across the road in front of us. I'm a soft hearted person by nature so my first instinct was to try and avoid it. As if reading my mind, Chris sternly told me to hit it. He had always advised me that, while driving full speed on the highway, never try to avoid hitting animals that step in front of you, be it a cat, dog or bird. He knew of people who got killed in smash ups trying to avoid hitting the random stray dog on the highway. I did as he advised and the chicken collided with the pick up at a velocity that surely killed it. ‘Pull to the side’ said Chris. He wanted to collect the dead bird to clean and cook when he got home later. I did as told, parked on the shoulder and reversed closer to where the dead bird lay. Chris got out to retrieve his spoils but after a minute he came back with an odd look on his face. ‘What?’ I said. He told me that I needed to see it for myself. I went with him to the bird and looked at it. Everything looked alright. Except for the fact that the bird was in a state whereby it had to have been dead for several hours. Its face and skin had that grey look of being long dead and there were ants coming out of its beak and an eyeless socket. ‘This can't be the chicken that we hit!’ I said. ‘It has to be another chicken that we hit! This one's already dead.’ Chris demonstrated to me that this was the exact location where we struck the chicken. There were feathers that got dislodged from the impact nearby that matched with our speckled bird. It was indeed our chicken. ‘This doesn't make any sense.’ I said stupified. Chris didn't think much about it. He was more focused on the disappointment that his roadkill was inedible. Zombie chickens crossing the road didn't seem to be of any concern to him. To this day I have no idea as to what could poossibly explain that supernatural event.

Did you ever stop caring about how old you are? I remember when I was 17 and the anxiety I felt knowing that in a few months I would be a full fledged adult with responsibilities. Ripe for work life, going steady and potential marriage. Reality: I was just a kid still going to school and nothing remotely resembling a girlfriend. I remember when I was 19 how much the prospect of turning 20 meant. The big 2–0 meant that I was a ‘hardback’ man planning his career, house and family. No time for shits and giggles. Reality: This was the most immature period of my life and I was far from any kind of career, house or family. I had more time than ever for shits and giggles. I remember at 25 I observed my hairline beginning to recede. I was paranoid that I was going bald. I felt like I would be seen as a balding old perv if I chatted up 18 yo girls in the mall. I thought I was no longer a youth. Reality: I was not a balding old perv but a young man with self esteem issues. At 30 I was working two jobs trying to make ends meet. I had a daughter and was in a troubled relationship with her mother. The last thing I cared about was how old I was and I haven’t put much thought to it since almost seven years later. The moral of my story is I would’ve enjoyed my life much better if I didn’t worry about age and age expectations the way I did as a youth. I am much less bothered about turning 40 than when I was about to turn 20. When the time comes I’ll be proud to know that I was lucky to live so long.

What is your scariest driving on a dark and lonely road at night story? A few years ago I had just finished shift doing pizza delivery. It was 11:30 pm at night. I hopped into my pickup and was heading my usual route home. The road I took was a sort of backroad that skirted several impoverished areas, hood, drug blocks and the like. As I made a bend at an area called Enterprise, infamous for an ongoing turf war between rival gangs I heard a frantic female voice screaming and yelling help. She was coming out of this track that led to a cluster of ugly, I'll kept shantytown houses. She looked between 25 — 32 and wore a nightgown. She deliriously ran towards me yelling in our local patios , 'Help, he go kill meh!’ There wasn't anyone behind her but I immediately stopped and beckoned for her to come into my vehicle. She stood there frozen for a moment. Suddenly this unnerving feeling that something was wrong had come over me and I realized that I had made a big mistake. I couldn't understand it but my instinct told me that I should drive off immediately. I saw a big burly man walking calmly towards her. 'Get in,' I shouted. However she just stood there paralyzed. Her fear was indeed real. She was not acting. I beckoned her inside again, all the while the burly man calmly walked towards her. She then gave me a look that I can never forget. She looked me in my eyes as though telling me that she didn't want to get me involved. That her fate was sealed. The man put his arm around her shoulder as though he were a husband comforting a delirious wife and walked her back into the track. I drove off. To this day I can't figure out what exactly happened that night. To this day I don't know what would've happened if she had indeed entered my vehicle but my instinct is grateful that she didn't. I would advise no one to stop and rescue screaming nightgowned women running out of dark, seedy tracks in the middle of the night.

What are the best episodes of the original Twilight Zone TV series? I think it's impossible to choose the best episodes of The Twilight Zone, however I can describe one of the most severely underrated. The Incredible World of Horace Ford No it's not scary. It's not spooky. It's barely even eerie. It's a profound reflection of changes of the past, childhood nostalgia and the how our ego manipulates many of us to believe 'things were so much better back then.’ *Spoiler Alert* Horace Ford is a gifted toy designer employed by a commercial toymaker. His talents stem from his ability to delve into the mind of a child and understand what appeals to them. However he's been having a midlife crisis of which, rather than brooding on the acceptance of incoming old age, he instead has mentally reverted back to that of a nine year old. He becomes silly and frivolous, neglects his job and throws tantrums whenever his employer and wife calmly try to reason with him. When he does open up about his problem he feverishly reminisces about the past, his old pals and how much simpler and better life was back then. His wife and boss try to explain to him that he is possibly fatigued and that he just needs to rest so he could get over this silly phase. Angered by their indifference he walks off his job and is magically transported back to his childhood. At first he is thrilled but gradually he is horrified to discover that his childhood was but a collection of poverty, overcrowded and dirty streets and his 'pals’ were mostly thuggish street urchins who bullied him. He is then transported back to the present where he confides to his wife what he saw and she reminds him that his childhood was actually traumatic but his ego manipulated him into believing it was great as a form of coping. He accepts the present and resumes his job, happy to find some closure in his life. Why I think it's great. Everyday we all hear a comment, whether online or in person of how much better things were in whatsoever decade. And so on and so on. Some of these comments are justified but many of them are coping mechanisms in regards to personal failures i.e. 'It's not that my life is a disappoinment. Life for everyone now is a disappoinment and here's the reasons why (refer to list above).’ I myself was guilty at some point of thinking like Horace Ford. That is until I chanced upon some old photos of me during childhood and it suddenly dawned on me things were better in a few aspects, but worse in many others. But no matter how bad things were, for many the ego would always try to romanticize the past and make it seem superior to the present. Baby boomers always talk about how great the 60s were despite the obvious issues of the period and their parents would speak highly of the 30s and 40s despite World War 2. This episode gives so much food for thought towards the question, 'Were things really all that great back then?’

Was Shelley Duvall considered attractive? When I was a boy growing up, this character was the epitome of ‘attractive’ among boys my age: This was the exact opposite: Now that I'm a full grown adult I find it odd that my attraction has reversed. Nowadays I would consider prime Shelley Duvall far more attractive than prime Pamela Anderson. I'm not saying this as a form of virtue signalling due to her sad passing. I've observed photos from her in the past and discovered that she possessed a very unique beauty. This beauty was exploited quite often in her roles and modeling in the 1970s. Sadly she was only given frumpy housewife and plain Jane supporting roles into the 80s and 90s and all but disappeared at the turn of the millenium, only resurfacing for that infamous Dr. Phil interview in 2016. Despite being tall and thin, with big ears and eyes and crooked teeth Shelley Duvall’s looks were all natural. This might be my personal opinion but she seemed to possess a certain humility about her; the kind of person who wouldn't put on airs about herself and be friendly to almost anyone. Pamela Anderson’s beauty involved a lot of plastic surgery, hair dye and excessive makeup. To each his own but in a hypothetical party full of people I'd make a bee line to be the first to offer a drink to Shelley Duvall. Then we'd talk, sit and laugh at all the hopelessly shallow guys flocking around Pamela Anderson at the other end of the room. RIP

What one thing did your father do that left your mother sobbing? Wasn't my biological father but my stepfather. Calling him 'stepfather’ is a bit of a compliment. He basically lived off my mom, was unemployed more often than not and barely provided anything for the rent free roof that lay above his head. Yet my mother persevered. She got involved with my biological father at a tender age and that relationship was traumatic due to his bipolar disorder. She was intent on having a proper family with my stepfather, especially after she bore him two daughters. As mentioned before he was more often unemployed and when when he did find a job it was temporary as he worked in construction. However, in the early 2000s he found some measure of success in the field and started getting established as a professional foreman. He got high paying, big contract jobs and had the power to hire and fire. Soon most of the guys in the street were given jobs by my stepfather and some of the neighborhood women sent love letters in the mailbox to my mother's ire. My stepfather would laugh it off. However as the months turned into years my mother calculated that with the amount of money my stepfather made, it wasn't reflected in the household. We were still broke, had almost no furniture, bills still piled up and the money he gave her was not any significant improvement to when he was roughing it. Things got worse when my stepfather would constantly disappear for the fortnight weekend, especially when he got his salary. When he gave my mother what scanty money remained in his wallet it led to ugly arguments. Everyone told my mother that my stepfather had to be seeing another woman. My mother refused to believe it. Instead she tried to nag, quarrel and harrass him into doing what was right and it just created more nasty arguments. She then resolved that he could no longer live with us but could see his daughters on the weekend. She believed this would change his ways. He readily agreed to this. One fateful Friday evening I was home and the phone rang. I answered it. I heard my stepfather's voice asking for 'Tracey.’ Tracey was the name of our neighbor's daughter. She was 24 years old and had a reputation. I said Tracey didn't live here. When my stepfather recognized my voice he immediately hung up the phone. My mother came and asked me who called. 'It's just S****n.’ 'What does he want?’ my mother said irritably. 'I dunno,' I replied, 'He just asked to talk to Tracey….I think he dialled the wrong number.’ At 16 years old I was a bit naive to comprehend what all this meant. However I'd never forget seeing my mother's face drop like she saw death materialize in front of her and later tears formed in her eyes. My stepfather was getting involved with our neighbor's daughter right across the street. That's where his money went. That meant everyone knew about it except her. That meant she was a fool. They parted ways permanently afterwards. My stepfather would demand that I say that I was mistaken. That it wasn't him who called. He's 68 now and his daughters want nothing to do with him. It really affected my mother as she became more withdrawn and a bit of a recluse and a hoarder. They both are barely on speaking terms. Sometimes I feel as though I should've had more common sense and just kept my mouth shut.

What screams "I'm low class"? A girl, no older than 20 comes into Papa John's a busy Friday evening. I'm helping out at the cash register. It's near the end of the month (pay day for most people) and this is when we get our bulk of orders. The phone is ringing off the hook. I'm really just a delivery guy but the store is short staffed so I help cash. The girl, her cellphone tucked at her groin area in her trousers comes up to me at the register. Totally ignoring the fact that I'm taking an order on the phone she proceeds to talk about what she wants. I paused from the phone call to tell her, ‘One minute please miss I'm on the phone with a customer.’ I look as her eyebrows slant further downwards in anger and she puts her arms on her hips, staring at me in a show of impatience. When I finished with the call I apologized and asked what would she like. ‘Gimme one of the chicken pizzas.’ The phone started ringing again. I sighed inwardly. All the time she spent staring at me in anger she didn't even make up her mind as to what she wanted. ‘Which one of the chicken pizzas?’ I don't know if by asking a simple question like that she found some measure of offense but she replied in a belligerent tone, ‘How am I supposed to know what chicken pizzas you have?’ The phone continued ringing. I sighed again. I pointed to the display above her head and told her I have to take the call, choose a pizza by the time. Instead she frowns at me while I take another phone order, she refusing to look at the menu board herself. When I was done she glared at me and said, ‘Chicken and pine….the largest size you have.’ ‘That would be an extra large’ I said. ‘I know!’ she spat. She then proceeds to take out of her purse a brown envelope which contained the salary she just received from whatever job she worked. She proudly counts her 100s in front of me and gave me $200 without waiting for me to tell her the price of her order. I gave her her change and receipt and told her the waiting time (15–20 mins). She proceeded to stare at me whilst I take other orders, helped cut pizzas from off the oven and organized my deliveries at the same time. With her seeing me doing all these things at once I thought she would have generated some sympathy for me seeing that I wasn't really the cashier but just a delivery guy helping out the situation. While heading towards the exit with my deliveries I passed near her and she beckons me. I thought it was to apologize for her attitude. Instead she tells me something that makes my blood boil instantly. ‘Ummm. How much longer for my order?’ She just placed her order 5 minutes ago! I gritted me teeth and replied, ‘It’s not in the oven yet. 10 to 15 minutes.’ She rolled her eyes and looked away. I then realize what her game was. She didn't really care about the pizza. Her fetish was to feel some sort of superiority over someone else and the only place she could achieve that was in a fast food restaurant. We get customers like that regularly, especially around month's end (pay day). They get some kind of sick thrill out of pissing people off and flaunting what (little) money they have. So to answer the question above, nothing screams 'I’m low class’ more than people who buy fast food for the sake of showing off/putting on airs.

What guitarists do you think have the most emotionally moving solos? I love this question because it's entirely subjective and for someone who has zero technical guitar knowledge and even less skills, I can answer it. It's rare that I sense a feeling of emotion in a guitar solo. Most solos to me just sound like cool improvisations that take you away from the rigidity of the melody and repetition of verse-chorus, verse-chorus. There are only a handful of songs that I've actually felt the emotion behind the playing. It's like the guitarist is talking to you with his guitar and you sense the emotions behind the words. Such are the best examples I can think of: Carlos Santana — Samba Pa Ti. This is possible the best example I can think of in regards to emotional solos. The entire song is basically an extended guitar solo. Wrought with the feelings of longing, regret and desire this song is one of the artist's most impressive contribution. I can hear a man at his wit's end wailing to lost love from the very first few notes. Buck Dharma — Don't Fear The Reaper Nothing is more terrifying than the ominous solo in this pre-heavy metal classic. I get visions of demonic creatures rising from beneath when this manic, blistering guitar starts going off after a creepy rhythm guitar intro. Buck Dharma wrote the song after envisioning death for himself and it shows in his playing. Jimi Hendrix — Little Wing Funny how this original composition grew from obscurity to one of his most covered songs. 'Fly on, Little Wing' Hendrix indeed takes us to soaring heights with this solo full of wonder, hope and optimism. I consider the solo an extension of the themes explored in another Hendrix classic The Wind Cries Mary. Play both solos one after the the other and you'll see what I mean. John Frusciante — Scar Tissue In the land of weeping guitars Scar Tissue reigns King. The greatest achievement of the Red Hot Chili Peppers in regards to their sombre, non funky output. Frusciante's guitar sounds like a broken down and dying animal. Figures that it is shown to be literally broken in the music video. Jonny Greenwood — Paranoid Android + There There Couldn't choose between the two Radiohead classics but they both explore the emotions of fear, paranoia and anxiety. Paranoid Android's solo is fractured yet blistering. It is cold and unconventional yet wrought with feelings, like an android having a physical and emotional breakdown. There There’s rhythm and solo combined instills a deeply fearful feeling of slowly incurring the wrath of some powerful unseen entity. And lastly Duane Allman — Melissa The slide guitar to end all slide guitar. A grandeur solo like no other is encapsulates themes of freedom, love and innocence. Duane's guitar makes its presence from the very beginning and soars to the heavens in its solo. Given the fact that Duane Allman died not long after creating this marvellous piece of work does one sense an almost spiritual connection with Duane's playing on this a masterpiece.
